prompt: In 1893, which self-governing country became the first in the world to give women the right to vote in national parliamentary elections?
explanation: New Zealand’s Electoral Act, signed into law on 19 September 1893, made women aged 21 and over eligible to vote in parliamentary elections, and more than 100,000 women enrolled within two months.
context: Women could not stand for Parliament until 1919, and the 1893 law covered Māori women on the same terms as other women, though some groups, such as Chinese women, were excluded. A few places had earlier given only some women a vote (Pitcairn Island in 1838, the Isle of Man in 1881), which is why historians say New Zealand was the first self-governing country to do so for women generally.

sources.title: Brief history of women’s suffrage in New Zealand
sources.publisher: NZHistory (New Zealand Ministry for Culture and Heritage)
sources.evidence: States the Electoral Act passed on 8 September 1893 and was signed by Lord Glasgow on 19 September, made women aged 21+ who were British subjects eligible to vote, extended the vote to Māori women on the same terms, excluded some groups such as Chinese women, and that women gained the right to stand for Parliament in 1919.

sources.title: Women’s Suffrage in Aotearoa New Zealand
sources.evidence: States New Zealand was the first self-governing country in the world to enshrine in law women’s right to vote in parliamentary elections, that the Act was signed on 19 September 1893, and that 109,461 women enrolled less than two months later.

sources.title: World suffrage timeline
sources.publisher: NZHistory (New Zealand Ministry for Culture and Heritage)
sources.evidence: Says New Zealand can justly claim to be the first self-governing country to grant the vote to all adult women, and lists earlier partial grants such as Pitcairn Island (1838) and the Isle of Man (1881, propertied women).

prompt: The 2015 Paris Agreement aims to hold global warming to well below which level, compared with pre-industrial times?
explanation: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement aims to hold the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.
context: The agreement was adopted in Paris on 12 December 2015 by the 196 parties to the UN climate convention. Each country sets its own national climate plan (called a nationally determined contribution), and each party must submit a new one every five years.

sources.title: The Paris Agreement (official text, FCCC/CP/2015/10/Add.1)
sources.publisher: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
sources.evidence: Article 2(1)(a) sets the aim of holding the temperature increase to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts toward 1.5 °C; the text was adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015 in Paris; Article 4(9) requires each party to communicate a nationally determined contribution every five years.

sources.title: Paris Climate Agreement to enter into force on 4 November
sources.evidence: Confirms the agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015 in Paris by the 196 parties to the UN climate convention, with the goal of keeping warming well below 2 °C and pursuing 1.5 °C.

prompt: In 2001, which country became the first in the world to legalise same-sex marriage?
explanation: The Netherlands was the first country to adopt same-sex marriage: at midnight on 1 April 2001, Amsterdam’s mayor Job Cohen married the first four same-sex couples.
context: Denmark was the first country to offer registered partnerships, in 1989, but those were not marriage. The Netherlands’ 2001 law was the first to open marriage itself to same-sex couples.

sources.title: Twenty years of marriage equality in NL: 20,000 married same-sex couples
sources.evidence: Says the Netherlands was the first country in the world to implement marriage equality in 2001 and that at midnight on 1 April 2001 Amsterdam mayor Job Cohen officiated the marriage of four same-sex couples.

sources.title: Access to registered same-sex partnerships: it’s a question of equality
sources.publisher: Council of Europe (Commissioner for Human Rights)
sources.evidence: Quotes the Commissioner saying the first country to provide registered partnerships was Denmark in 1989 and that the Netherlands was first to adopt same-sex marriage, in 2001.

prompt: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a landmark statement of the fundamental rights every person holds, was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in which year?
explanation: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948. The UN describes it as setting out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected.
context: A drafting committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt included members from eight countries. The Declaration is not legally binding, but it has inspired many later human rights treaties. 10 December is observed each year as Human Rights Day.

sources.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
sources.evidence: States the General Assembly proclaimed the Declaration in Paris on 10 December 1948 (resolution 217 A), that it sets out for the first time fundamental human rights to be universally protected, and that it was drafted by representatives from different legal and cultural backgrounds.

sources.title: History of the Declaration
sources.evidence: Confirms adoption on 10 December 1948 in Paris and that the drafting committee, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, drew its members from eight States.

sources.title: Human Rights Day
sources.publisher: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
sources.evidence: States Human Rights Day is 10 December, marking the 1948 adoption of the UDHR, and that the UDHR is not a binding document but has inspired more than 60 human rights instruments.

prompt: Who became South Africa’s first democratically elected president in 1994, after the end of apartheid?
explanation: After South Africa’s first national democratic elections in April 1994, the new National Assembly elected Nelson Mandela president on 9 May 1994, and he was sworn in on 10 May at the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
context: Mandela had spent 27 years in prison. He and outgoing president F. W. de Klerk shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize for helping end apartheid peacefully and laying the foundations for a new, democratic South Africa.

sources.title: Parliament elected Mandela 20 years ago
sources.evidence: States the National Assembly elected Mandela President on Monday 9 May 1994 (nominated by Albertina Sisulu, no other nominations), the day before his inauguration in Pretoria, following the ANC’s victory in South Africa’s first democratic elections.

sources.title: Nelson Mandela inaugurated as South Africa’s first democratic president
sources.evidence: States Mandela was sworn in on 10 May 1994 at the Union Buildings, following the April 1994 first national democratic elections, replacing F. W. de Klerk as president, and that he spent 27 years in jail.

sources.title: The Nobel Peace Prize 1993 – Press release
sources.evidence: States the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded jointly to Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk for their work to end apartheid peacefully and lay the foundations for a new democratic South Africa.

prompt: A landmark UN treaty adopted in 2006, described by the UN as the first comprehensive human rights treaty of the 21st century, protects the rights of which group?
explanation: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was adopted on 13 December 2006 and entered into force on 3 May 2008.
context: The Convention marks a shift away from treating people with disabilities as objects of charity, medical treatment and social protection, towards recognising them as people with rights who can make decisions about their own lives.

sources.title: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD)
sources.publisher: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs
sources.evidence: States the Convention was adopted on 13 December 2006 at UN Headquarters, entered into force on 3 May 2008, is called the first comprehensive human rights treaty of the 21st century, and shifts from viewing persons with disabilities as objects of charity and medical treatment to subjects with rights.

sources.title: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
sources.publisher: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs
sources.evidence: Confirms adoption on 13 December 2006, entry into force on 3 May 2008, and the description as the first comprehensive human rights treaty of the 21st century.

prompt: On 13 May 1888, Brazil abolished slavery with a law known by which name?

options.text: Lei do Ventre Livre (Law of the Free Womb)

explanation: The Lei Áurea (Law No. 3,353) declared slavery extinct in Brazil from 13 May 1888. It was signed by Princess Isabel, who was acting as regent while Emperor Pedro II was abroad. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery.
context: Earlier laws only chipped away at slavery: the 1850 Eusébio de Queirós law banned the slave trade, the 1871 Free Womb law freed children born to enslaved mothers from that year on, and the Sexagenarians Law freed enslaved people over 60. The Lei Áurea gave freed people no compensation or state assistance.

sources.title: Confira a íntegra da Lei Áurea
sources.evidence: Reproduces Lei n. 3.353 of 13 May 1888, whose first article declares slavery extinct in Brazil from the date of the law, signed by the Princess Imperial Regent.

sources.title: Congresso teve papel fundamental em processo abolicionista
sources.evidence: Describes the 1850 Eusébio de Queiroz law banning the slave trade, the 1871 Free Womb law (children of enslaved mothers born from that year free), a law freeing enslaved people over 60, and the Lei Áurea of 1888.

sources.title: Há 131 anos, senadores aprovavam o fim da escravidão no Brasil
sources.evidence: Says the Lei Áurea abolished slavery on 13 May 1888 and that Princess Isabel sanctioned it while acting as regent with Emperor Pedro II abroad.

sources.title: Forced labour in Brazil: 120 years after the abolition of slavery, the fight goes on
sources.evidence: States Brazil formally ended slavery on 13 May 1888, making it the final country in the Americas to do so.

sources.title: Lei Áurea
sources.evidence: Supplementary: says the law gave freed people no compensation or state assistance, and that Princess Isabel signed it as regent on 13 May 1888.

prompt: Saudi Arabia ended its ban on women driving in June 2018.
explanation: Real. The ban was lifted on 24 June 2018, nine months after the decision was announced by royal decree in September 2017.
context: Activists who had campaigned for the right to drive were arrested in the weeks before the ban ended, and were reported to still be in prison when it took effect.

sources.title: Saudi women hit the road as driving ban is lifted
sources.evidence: Reports that the driving ban was lifted on Sunday 24 June 2018, after a royal decree announced in September 2017, and that activists who campaigned for the right had been arrested in preceding weeks.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia's ban on women driving officially ends
sources.evidence: Dated 24 June 2018; reports Saudi women are now officially allowed to drive, the change having been announced the previous September, and that Saudi Arabia had been the only country barring women from driving.

prompt: In 2022, Costa Rica generated more than 98% of its electricity from renewable sources.
explanation: Real. Data from Costa Rica’s national electricity control centre showed 99.25% of electricity came from renewables in 2022 (1 January to 20 December), mostly hydropower, geothermal and wind.
context: This is about electricity only, not all energy use. Reports said it was the eighth year in a row with more than 98% renewable electricity. Hydropower supplied about three quarters of the total in 2022.

sources.title: Este 2022 Costa Rica produjo un 99,25% de su electricidad a partir de fuentes renovables
sources.evidence: Reports 99.25% renewable electricity in 2022 (1 Jan to 20 Dec) from CENCE/ICE data: hydro 75.16%, geothermal 12.97%, wind 10.65%, biomass and solar 0.47%; eighth straight year above 98%.

sources.title: Costa Rica exceeds 98% renewable electricity generation for the eighth consecutive year
sources.evidence: Published 22 December 2022; states Costa Rica’s electricity generation exceeded 98% renewable for the eighth consecutive year.

prompt: The Antarctic ozone hole was caused mainly by carbon dioxide emissions.
explanation: Fake. The ozone hole forms through reactions involving chlorine and bromine, which come primarily from CFCs, chemicals once used in products such as refrigerants and aerosols. Carbon dioxide drives climate change, a separate problem.
context: Nations signed the Montreal Protocol two years after the hole was discovered in 1985. A 2023 UN-backed assessment said the ozone layer is on track to recover to 1980 levels around 2066 over Antarctica if current policies continue.

sources.title: Ozone Hole Watch
sources.evidence: States that chemical reactions involving chlorine and bromine destroy ozone over the southern polar region in the Southern Hemisphere spring.

sources.title: NASA Study: First Direct Proof of Ozone Hole Recovery Due to Chemicals Ban
sources.evidence: States that the chlorine and bromine driving the ozone hole come primarily from CFCs, that the Montreal Protocol was signed two years after the 1985 discovery, and that full recovery will take decades.

sources.title: Ozone layer on track to heal within decades, UN report finds
sources.evidence: Reports the 2023 UN assessment: recovery to 1980 levels around 2066 over Antarctica, 2045 over the Arctic and 2040 elsewhere, credited to the phase-out of ozone-depleting chemicals under the Montreal Protocol.

prompt: Women in Switzerland have been able to vote in national elections since 1920.
explanation: Fake. Swiss women gained the right to vote and stand in national elections after a referendum on 7 February 1971, in which only men could vote; about 65.7% approved.
context: Cantonal rights lagged further: Appenzell Innerrhoden, the last canton, only gave women equal political rights in 1990 after the Federal Supreme Court ruled that excluding them violated the constitution. Women there first voted in a cantonal assembly in April 1991.

sources.title: Right of women to vote and participate in elections 1971
sources.publisher: Swiss Federal Commission for Women’s Issues (EKF)
sources.evidence: States that on 7 February 1971 Swiss men with voting rights approved women’s right to vote and stand in national elections, and that Appenzell Innerrhoden, the last canton, granted women equal political rights in 1990.

sources.title: 50 Years of Women’s Suffrage in Switzerland
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis
sources.evidence: Says 65.7% of male voters approved federal women’s suffrage on 7 February 1971; the Federal Supreme Court ruling in 1990 on Appenzell Innerrhoden; women there first voted on 28 April 1991.

prompt: In 2008, Rwanda became the first country in the world whose lower house of parliament had a majority of women.
explanation: Real. After its 2008 election, 45 of the 80 seats (56.3%) in Rwanda’s Chamber of Deputies were held by women, described by the IPU as the first single or lower house in history with a women’s majority.
context: Rwanda uses a quota system, and 24 of the 80 seats are in effect reserved for women. The IPU’s Parline database currently lists women at about 64% of the lower house. Parliamentary numbers alone do not measure women’s equality in wider society.

sources.title: Press conference by Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU)
sources.evidence: Reports Rwanda topped the world list in 2008 with 56% of lower-house seats held by women, and that a quota system means 24 of 80 seats are effectively reserved for women.

sources.title: Rwanda – Chamber of Deputies
sources.evidence: Currently lists 63.75% of lower-house members as women.

prompt: Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir, who became Iceland’s first female prime minister in 2009, married her female partner in 2010.
explanation: Real. Sigurðardóttir was sworn in as prime minister on 1 February 2009 and married Jónína Leósdóttir on 27 June 2010, the day same-sex marriage became legal in Iceland.
context: She was widely reported as the world’s first openly gay head of government. Britannica notes that Per-Kristian Foss briefly served as acting prime minister of Norway in 2002, so the “first” label is not undisputed.

sources.title: First gay prime minister takes office in Iceland
sources.evidence: Reports Sigurdardottir took office as prime minister of Iceland, its first female prime minister and first openly gay national leader of modern times.

sources.title: Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir
sources.evidence: States she served 2009 to 2013, was sworn in on 1 February 2009, and on 27 June 2010 married Jónína Leósdóttir the day same-sex marriage became legal; notes the Foss nuance.

prompt: Te reo Māori has never been an official language of New Zealand.
explanation: Fake. Section 3 of the Māori Language Act 1987 declared Māori an official language of New Zealand, and the Act came into force on 1 August 1987.
context: The Act also created the Māori Language Commission, renamed Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori in 1991. It followed a 1985 Waitangi Tribunal finding that te reo is a taonga the Crown must protect. The 1987 Act was later replaced by the Māori Language Act 2016.

sources.title: Māori Language Act 1987
sources.evidence: Section 3 declares the Māori language an official language of New Zealand; notes the Act was repealed on 30 April 2016 by the Māori Language Act 2016.

sources.title: Māori becomes an official language
sources.publisher: NZHistory (NZ Ministry for Culture and Heritage)
sources.evidence: States the Act came into force on 1 August 1987 making te reo Māori official, set up the Māori Language Commission (renamed in 1991), following a 1985 Waitangi Tribunal finding that te reo is a taonga.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I was born in 1940 in Nyeri, Kenya, and in 1971 I earned a PhD from the University of Nairobi.
In 1977 I founded a grassroots movement that encouraged women to plant trees.
In 2004 I became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
explanation: Wangari Maathai (1940–2011) founded the Green Belt Movement, which links tree planting with women’s empowerment, environmental protection and democracy.
context: Britannica notes she was effectively the first woman in East or Central Africa to earn a doctorate. After the 2002 elections she served as Kenya’s Assistant Minister for Environment, Natural Resources and Wildlife.

sources.title: Wangari Maathai – Biographical
sources.evidence: Born 1940 in Nyeri, Kenya; PhD from the University of Nairobi in 1971; 2004 Nobel Peace Prize; appointed Assistant Minister for Environment, Natural Resources and Wildlife after the December 2002 election.

sources.title: Wangari Maathai – Speed read
sources.evidence: Green Belt Movement founded on 5 June 1977; Maathai was the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize (2004).

sources.title: Wangari Maathai
sources.evidence: Born 1 April 1940 in Nyeri; PhD in 1971, effectively the first woman in East or Central Africa with a doctorate; movement founded 1977 and had planted some 30 million trees by the early 21st century.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I am an organisation that began in London in 1961.
I grew from an appeal published in a British newspaper by a lawyer, calling on the public to act for people jailed for peacefully expressing their beliefs.
In 1977 I won the Nobel Peace Prize.
explanation: Amnesty International grew from Peter Benenson’s 1961 appeal “The Forgotten Prisoners”, published in The Observer, which popularised the term “prisoners of conscience”.
context: The appeal prompted letter-writing groups in several countries to form. Delegates from seven countries met in July 1961 to set up a permanent international movement, which took the name Amnesty International the following year.

sources.title: Amnesty International
sources.evidence: Founded in London on 28 May 1961 by Peter Benenson, a British lawyer; awarded the 1977 Nobel Peace Prize.

sources.title: Amnesty International: Our history
sources.evidence: In 1961 British lawyer Peter Benenson wrote “The Forgotten Prisoners” for the Observer, launching the Appeal for Amnesty; Amnesty received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.

sources.title: The Appeal for Amnesty campaign is launched
sources.evidence: Benenson’s article appeared on the Observer front page in May 1961, urged protest on behalf of people jailed for peaceful expression, popularised “prisoners of conscience”; delegates from seven countries met in July and the body became Amnesty International the next year.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I was a mathematician who began working for NASA’s predecessor agency, NACA, in 1953.
Before his 1962 orbital flight, an astronaut asked for me by name to check the computer’s trajectory calculations.
A 2016 film called Hidden Figures tells part of my story.
explanation: Katherine Johnson’s calculations supported early American crewed spaceflights; John Glenn asked for her to verify the computer’s numbers before his 1962 Friendship 7 orbital flight.
context: She worked in Langley’s all-Black West Area Computing section, led by Dorothy Vaughan. President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.

sources.title: Katherine Johnson Biography
sources.evidence: Hired by NACA in June 1953; worked in the all-Black West Area Computing section led by Dorothy Vaughan; Glenn asked for her to check the orbital calculations before flying; Medal of Freedom in 2015.

sources.title: Katherine Johnson
sources.evidence: Glenn asked her to double-check the electronic computer’s trajectories before his 1962 Friendship 7 flight; Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015; Taraji P. Henson played her in the 2016 film Hidden Figures.

sources.title: When Did John Glenn Ask for ‘the Girl’ to Check the Numbers?
sources.evidence: Friendship 7 launched on 20 February 1962; Glenn’s request came shortly before launch, though the exact date is undocumented.

In 2012 I was shot by the Taliban on my way home from school because I campaigned for girls’ education.
In 2014, aged 17, I became the youngest person ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I was born in 1944 in Xapuri, in the Brazilian state of Acre, and began tapping rubber as a boy.
I organised rubber tappers to resist the clearing of Amazon forest for cattle ranching, using non-violent human blockades.
I was murdered in 1988, and a Brazilian federal biodiversity agency created in 2007 carries my name.
explanation: Chico Mendes led the rubber tappers’ union in Xapuri and became a symbol of the link between forest protection and the rights of forest workers.
context: His blockades, called empates, used people’s bodies to stop trees from being felled. He was shot dead outside his home on 22 December 1988. Brazil’s Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio) was created by Law 11.516 of 28 August 2007.

sources.title: Mendes Filho, Francisco (“Chico”) Alves (1944–1988)
sources.evidence: Born 15 December 1944 in Acre (native town Xapuri); tapped rubber from age eleven; led the Xapuri union; used the empate, a human blockade, against clearing for ranchers; killed 22 December 1988.

sources.title: Chico Mendes
sources.evidence: Born 1944 in Xapuri, Acre; used human blockades (empates) against deforestation; shot dead outside his home in Xapuri in December 1988.

sources.title: Lei nº 11.516 de 28/08/2007
sources.evidence: Law 11.516 of 28 August 2007 creates the Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade.

sources.title: Brazil salutes Chico Mendes 25 years after murder
sources.evidence: Born 1944; began tapping rubber as a child; killed on 22 December 1988 in Xapuri by a rancher’s shot.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I am a K’iche’ Maya woman from Guatemala.
My brother and mother were killed by Guatemala’s security forces in 1979–1980, and I went into exile in Mexico in 1981.
In 1992 I won the Nobel Peace Prize for my work for the rights of Indigenous peoples.
explanation: Rigoberta Menchú Tum, born in 1959, became an international advocate for Indigenous rights and ethno-cultural reconciliation, and used her Nobel prize money to found a foundation for Indigenous peoples.
context: Her autobiography became an influential account of army atrocities in Guatemala’s civil war. After a 1999 critique of parts of it, the Nobel Committee said the prize was not based mainly on the book and did not revoke it.

sources.title: Rigoberta Menchú Tum – Biographical
sources.evidence: Born 9 January 1959 into a Maya (Quiché) peasant family; family members killed by security forces 1979–1980; exile in Mexico in 1981; 1992 Nobel Peace Prize for advocacy of Indigenous rights; Committee rejected calls to revoke the prize after the 1999 critique of her book.

sources.title: Rigoberta Menchú
sources.evidence: Guatemalan Quiché (K’iche’) Maya activist; 1992 Nobel Peace Prize; brother killed by a military death squad in 1979, mother murdered in 1980; fled to Mexico in 1981; founded an Indigenous advocacy organisation with the prize money.

prompt: Who am I?
clues: I was a British mathematician who worked at Bletchley Park during the Second World War on breaking German Enigma messages.
In 1950 I published a paper proposing an “imitation game” to ask whether machines can think, an idea now often named after me.
I was convicted in 1952 for homosexual acts, which were then illegal, and received a royal pardon in 2013.
explanation: Alan Turing was a founder of computer science and artificial intelligence, whose wartime work was central to breaking the Enigma code.
context: After his 1952 conviction he lost his security clearance and was made to undergo hormone treatment; he died in 1954. The UK government’s pardon took effect on 24 December 2013.

sources.title: Royal pardon for WW2 code-breaker Dr Alan Turing
sources.evidence: Worked at Bletchley Park and was central to breaking Enigma; convicted in 1952 of homosexual activity, then illegal; pardon granted on 24 December 2013; lost security clearance.

sources.title: Alan Turing, who cracked Nazi code, gets posthumous pardon
sources.evidence: Convicted of gross indecency in 1952; required to take estrogen; died in 1954; Queen Elizabeth II issued a posthumous pardon in December 2013.

sources.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (Mind, October 1950)
sources.evidence: Copy of Turing’s paper in Mind, Vol. LIX, No. 236, October 1950, introducing the “imitation game”.
